job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Carla Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carla, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior technician at an electrical contractor in Ashford Vale. I studied electrical engineering, and my placement was a summer on a substation upgrade. Now I draw wiring plans for new housing estates, check them against the regulations and visit a site twice a week with a senior electrician, Mr Doyle. I share a flat with two girls from my church choir, and I sing on Sundays. My boyfriend Samir and I hope to get engaged next year, but the loan and the rent make that feel far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let it be slow. A job is a dignity, and I'd rather see people keep their work than see companies chase every fashion. At church people would ask me what I think, and I'd say it's mostly noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still worry. My loan is huge, my pay is low and I have under a month of savings. Even in a calm world, one cancelled housing project and I'm the junior they let go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to site with Mr Doyle and learn everything I can by watching, because the regulations are what make me useful. I'd put 40 a month aside from my pay, and I'd keep my budget in a paper notebook like my mother taught me. I'd also not touch any AI tool, since I prefer to understand a drawing from the ground up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but tired. Like carrying a bag that gets heavier every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd cut first is the new coat I wanted and the bus pass, so I'd walk. Samir and I would keep our dates cheap, a walk and a flask of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost the job, who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lost my job, I'd ask Mr Doyle for a reference, then go to my pastor and the choir for help finding something. Our community looks after its own, and that's a comfort I try not to take for granted.

say: I'd say **slow** is good, because a job is a dignity and companies shouldn't chase every fashion.
At church I'd call it mostly **noise**.
think: My loan is huge, my pay is low and I have under a month of **savings**.
One cancelled housing project and I'm the **junior** they let go first.
do: Keep going to **site** with Mr Doyle and learn by watching.
Put **40** a month aside and keep a paper budget notebook.
Skip **AI tools** and understand each drawing from the ground up.
feel: I feel **steady** but tired, like carrying a bag that gets heavier every week.
S0.quote: Our community looks after its own, and that's a comfort I try not to take for granted.
fieldNote: Carla's security is **community and faith**, which she names as a comfort more than her pay.
She rejects AI tools and prizes the regulations she learns on site.
Even in the calm scenario her debt and thin savings keep her anxious.

steps.text: Keep joining Mr Doyle on site visits and learn the regulations
Put 40 a month aside in a paper-budget savings jar
Walk to work instead of buying the bus pass
Ask the pastor and choir to help find work if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should not be careless with people's livelihoods. Companies that use AI to cut staff should have to show they've also trained them for something else. At church I'd say that work is part of how we take care of our families, and no machine should push that aside lightly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is partly in the firing line. The drawing and checking I do is exactly what software can learn. But the site visits and the real wiring need a person, so I might be safer than someone who sits all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Doyle to take me on as a proper apprentice for the site work, so I'm learning the hands-on side. I'd stay away from AI, but if the firm buys a drawing program, I'd learn it from a colleague who's willing. I'd also save 60 a month and speak to my pastor about a small fund the congregation has for young families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Like when the weather changes before a procession. I trust that we will manage, but I can't say how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you worried about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I worry about is the young people who don't have a community behind them. My flatmate Hana has no church, and her family lives abroad. If she loses her job, she has nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a company to do before it cuts staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hana to come with me to choir and meet people. Meeting people sounds small, but that's how a person survives a hard year.

say: I'd say companies must not be careless with **livelihoods** and should train people they replace.
At church I'd say work is how we **care for families**.
think: The drawing and checking I do is exactly what software can **learn**.
The site visits and wiring need a **person**, so I may be safer than desk workers.
do: Ask Mr Doyle to take me on as a proper **apprentice** for site work.
Learn any new drawing program from a willing **colleague**.
Save **60** a month and ask my pastor about the congregation's fund.
feel: I feel **unsettled**, like weather changing before a procession.
S1.quote: Meeting people sounds small, but that's how a person survives a hard year.
fieldNote: Carla puts **community and apprenticeship** at the centre, with hands-on site work as her protection.
She worries about a flatmate with no church or family nearby, showing how much her own safety net matters.
She resists AI tools but accepts workplace training when others lead.

steps.text: Ask Mr Doyle to take me on as a formal apprentice
Save 60 a month toward my loan
Speak to my pastor about the congregation's fund for young families
Learn any drawing program the firm buys from a willing colleague

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much, too fast. At church I'd ask for prayer and also for practical help, and I'd say the government and firms must not leave ordinary families on their own. I'd tell my boss that no one should be let go without time to find something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. My job is drawings and regulations, which a machine can do in minutes. I'd have two years, a big loan and a boyfriend who works in a bakery, and neither of us has savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost I can and move back into my aunt's flat, which is small, but she's said I'm always welcome. I'd put off the engagement and the wedding, and that would hurt me. I'd apply for any job on site or in maintenance, because the robots for that are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, and angry too. I did what a good daughter does, studied hard and worked, and now it might be taken away. I'd pray a lot, and I'd cry on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the delay mean for you and Samir?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samir and I would have to put the engagement on hold. He says he'll wait, but I don't want my boyfriend Samir waiting for a life that never starts. That's the thing I think about most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be hard to ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my pastor for help with a food parcel if it came to that, though I'd be embarrassed. Pride is a luxury I'd have to put down.

say: I'd say it's **too much, too fast**, and nobody should be let go without time.
At church I'd ask for **prayer** and practical help.
think: My drawings and regulations are what a machine does in **minutes**.
I'd have two years, a big loan and **no savings**, and Samir has none either.
do: Cut every cost and move into my **aunt's** small flat.
Apply for any **site or maintenance** job, since robots arrive later there.
feel: I feel **afraid** and angry, since I did what a good daughter does.
S2.quote: I don't want my boyfriend Samir waiting for a life that never starts.
fieldNote: Carla's fear is **personal and family-centred**: the engagement, her aunt's flat, her pastor.
Pride is her main obstacle to asking for help.
She expects to lose her thinking job quickly and has no savings.

steps.text: Move into my aunt's small flat to cut rent
Put off the engagement and wedding with Samir
Apply for site and maintenance electrical jobs
Ask my pastor about a food parcel if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is time to do the right thing. I'd say that families and churches should help each other, and that firms must train people instead of just letting them go. I'd say we should support apprenticeships, because they are how a person gets a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved. By 2031 I'd be 27, married, I hope, and I'd know a trade that robots would take longer to learn. But I'd be anxious that the firms won't wait, and that the government won't be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship with Mr Doyle and get my electrician's licence, which is a proper qualification. I'd save 100 a month and put half of it toward the loan. And I'd go ahead with my engagement in 2028, but a small one, in the church hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, in a quiet way. Like when the choir finally finds the right note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if five years turned out to be three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If five years became three, I'd be midway through my licence and I'd have to scramble. I'd hold on to the hands-on side and stay close to the people who know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the wedding look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Samir and our families to help with a plain wedding. We're not interested in fuss. A wedding in a church hall with tea and cake is perfect.

say: I'd say five years is time to do the **right thing**, and firms must train people, not discard them.
I'd back **apprenticeships**, because that is how a person gets a trade.
think: By 2031 I'd be 27 and know a **trade** robots take longer to learn.
I'd be anxious that firms **won't wait** and the government won't be ready.
do: Finish my **apprenticeship** and get my electrician's licence.
Save **100** a month, putting half toward the loan.
Hold a small **engagement** in the church hall in 2028.
feel: I feel **calmer**, like when the choir finally finds the right note.
S3.quote: A wedding in a church hall with tea and cake is perfect.
fieldNote: Carla uses the extra time to get a **trade licence**, linking work and family plans together.
She keeps a plain, community-based picture of the good life.
Anxiety remains because debt is high and she doubts firms and government will keep pace.

steps.text: Finish the apprenticeship and get an electrician's licence
Save 100 a month and pay half toward the loan
Hold a small engagement in the church hall in 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time, and I'd say that we should use it well. I'd tell friends it's a chance for families to plan, and for firms to train. I'd also say to the government that apprenticeships should be paid properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, with a family, a licence and a steady trade. I might still be uneasy about the technology, but I'd have time to see what works and what doesn't before I'm forced to try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a licensed electrician and work towards supervising a team. I'd save for a deposit on a small house near the church. I'd marry Samir and hopefully have a child by the end of the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, honestly. Ten years gives a family a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about your future children's world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me is the world my children would grow up in. I'd want my children to learn a trade and also a faith, so they can stand on something. That's the real security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd ask of employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could ask for one thing, it would be that employers keep faith with the people who give them years of work. I don't think that's a lot.

I'd say apprenticeships should be **paid properly**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 with a **family**, a licence and a steady trade.
I'd have time to see what works before I'm **forced** to try new technology.
do: Become a licensed **electrician** and aim to supervise a team.
Save for a **deposit** on a small house near the church.
Marry **Samir** and hope for a child by the end of the decade.
feel: I feel **peaceful**, because ten years gives a family a chance.
S4.quote: I'd want my children to learn a trade and also a faith, so they can stand on something.
fieldNote: Carla's picture is **settled and communal**: licence, house, marriage, children, church.
She doesn't have to use AI until it is proven, and ten years gives her that time.
The calm comes from the long runway, not from any change in her debts.

steps.text: Qualify as a licensed electrician and aim to supervise a team
Save for a deposit on a small house near the church
Marry Samir and plan for a child before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My loan, my rent, and no savings would meet a world that moves too fast for my family and my church to respond. What would help is paid apprenticeships, an employer who keeps faith with me and a community that holds its own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of work, just of being treated as disposable. People like me don't ask for handouts, but we do ask for a fair chance to earn.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of work, just of being treated as disposable.
portrait: Carla is a **junior electrical technician** in Ashford Vale, singing in her church choir and sharing a flat with two friends.
She is **traditional** and resistant to change, avoids AI tools and trusts the regulations she learns on site.
Her safety net is **community**: her pastor, aunt and choir, though pride makes it hard to ask.
Her engagement and **family plans** rise and fall with how much time the scenario gives.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because her debt, rent and engagement plans meet a job a machine can do quickly.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships**, employers who keep faith with their people and a community that holds its own.
